I’ve been farming these fields for 50 years, since I was 20. My old woman and me, we’re both over 70 now, and it’s just the two of us in the house. Our children are working in Shijiazhuang — they send a little money when they can, but I don’t count on it. We have 24 mu, and we do wheat and corn, back to back, same as everyone in the village.

The corn just came off the field last week. Yield was decent, about 900 jin per mu. Now the ground is dry and I need to get the wheat in quick. I hired Lao Zhang’s son to bring his tractor for rotary tillage. I sold my own tractor five years ago — too old to fix it, and my back can’t take the bouncing anymore. We’ll drill the wheat seed by October 10th if the weather holds. I bought 600 jin of improved wheat seed, about 25 jin per mu. I don’t buy new seed every year; after two years of saving my own, it’s time to refresh so the seedlings come up strong and even.

For fertilizer, I bought 25 bags of compound fertilizer, each bag is 40 kg. That works out to a bit more than one bag per mu — about 40 kg per mu — which I spread before planting and the tractor works in. Then at Qingming, around early April, if the wheat looks a bit yellow, I topdress with urea — about 35 to 40 jin per mu, which is around 18 kg. Last year I tried to save money and used only 25 jin of urea, and the wheat was thin at jointing. I lost more than I saved. This year I won’t cut back. My neighbor Wang used the full amount and his yield was better, so I’ll do the same as him.

I irrigate the wheat three times. First, before winter sets in, so the wheat can survive the cold. Second, when it turns green in March. Third, when the heads come out in late April or early May. Each time costs me electricity for the pump, about 20 yuan per mu. It’s not cheap, but without water there’s no grain. I don’t water more than three times — my old bones can’t handle moving those pipes every week, and the electricity bill adds up.

For pesticides, I spray herbicide once in the spring when the wheat is still low. I don’t usually need insecticide for wheat, but I watch for aphids. If they come heavy, I’ll spray; if not, I save the money.

Come June, as soon as the wheat is off — usually around June 10th — I have to get the corn in immediately. There’s no time to plow. We plant directly behind the combine. I buy hybrid corn seed, Zhengdan 958, about 6 jin per mu. You can’t save corn seed, everyone knows that. I put down compound fertilizer in the row at planting, about half a bag per mu — around 25 kg. Then when the corn is up to my knee, at the big trumpet stage in late July, I broadcast urea, about 40 jin per mu. I irrigate twice for corn if the summer is dry — once with the topdress, and once in August when the ears are filling. If it rains enough, maybe only once, but I budget for twice.

For corn pests, I always use herbicide at planting, and I watch for corn borers in August. If I see them, I spray insecticide. Last year they weren’t bad, so I hope this year is the same.

Labor is tight. My wife and I do the fertilizing by hand, move the irrigation pipes, and watch the fields. For harvest, I hire two young men from the village to help load the grain onto the cart. That’s about 5 or 6 days for wheat, and 3 or 4 days for corn. They charge 150 yuan per day now. I also pay for the custom tractor and combine. Everything together — seed, fertilizer, electricity, pesticides, machinery, and hired hands — I figure I’ll spend about 19,000 yuan on inputs this year. That’s most of my cash. I keep 3,000 yuan aside in the tin box. Last year my cousin spent every yuan on fertilizer and then his wife got sick and he had to borrow money at high interest. I learned from that. I’d rather apply a little too much fertilizer and waste some money than apply too little and risk a bad year, but I’m not spending my last coin.

I expect the wheat to give me about 800 jin per mu, and the corn about 900 jin per mu, if the weather is normal. I’m not trying to get rich. I just want enough to live, pay for medicine, and not have to ask my children for help.
